analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict their advertising, and require stronger health warnings.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let the FDA regulate tobacco, backed by 97 House cosponsors from both parties, died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court ruled in March 2000 that the FDA had no legal authority to regulate tobacco, this bill would have written that authority into law. It would treat nicotine as a drug and tobacco products as devices under federal food and drug law, require stronger warning labels within 18 months, restrict tobacco advertising and promotion, and bar companies from claiming a cigarette is 'reduced risk' unless the FDA agrees. It deliberately carved tobacco farmers out of FDA oversight. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, especially young people. The FDA could restrict how tobacco is marketed, require the stronger warnings negotiated in the 1997 state settlement, stop companies from marketing 'light' or 'reduced-harm' cigarettes without proof, and revive the 1996 rules that restricted youth access to cigarettes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines nicotine in a tobacco product as a 'drug' and a tobacco product as a 'device' under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, giving the FDA legal authority to regulate them for the first time.
It validates the FDA's 1996 tobacco rules, which had been struck down by the Supreme Court, so they would take effect under the new statutory authority.

Within 18 months the Secretary of Health and Human Services must issue regulations requiring the stronger cigarette and smokeless tobacco warnings specified in the 1997 proposed settlement between tobacco manufacturers and state attorneys general.

Manufacturers could not claim in labeling or ads that a product poses a reduced health risk unless the FDA determined it actually significantly reduces risk, closing the 'light' and 'low-tar' marketing channel.
FDA sale-and-distribution restrictions would expressly include tobacco advertising and promotion, applied uniformly to all retailers, with no special exemption for stores that sell mostly tobacco.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, which would face FDA authority over their products, advertising limits, new warning requirements, and a bar on unproven reduced-risk claims. Tobacco farmers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives were explicitly shielded from any FDA oversight.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local rules: once a federal warning is required, no state could require any additional health statement on tobacco packages or ads, limiting states from going further than Washington.

It exempts tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority entirely, and even bars FDA employees from entering a tobacco farm without the owner's written consent, so the agricultural side of the industry stays outside federal health oversight.

It repeals the existing Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act and Smokeless Tobacco Act once the new warning rules take effect, replacing the old regime with a new one whose details depend on FDA rulemaking.

It does not treat tobacco like an ordinary drug that must prove safety: an action 'appropriate for the protection of public health' is deemed to provide reasonable assurance of safety, a deliberately weaker standard that stops short of a product ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large: tobacco products kill more than 400,000 Americans a year by the bill's own findings, and FDA authority would let regulators restrict marketing, especially to young people, and police false 'light' claims. The costs fall almost entirely on tobacco companies and their advertisers. The main honest criticisms are design compromises, not the goal: the preemption of stricter state warnings and the blanket farmer exemption are concessions that narrow what the law would cover.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee in April 2000, and it sat there until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 6, 2000, by Representative Greg Ganske, a Republican, with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including John Dingell and Henry Waxman among Democrats and Christopher Cox and Jim Leach among Republicans.

Its findings state that tobacco products are addictive, cause over 400,000 deaths each year, and that the Supreme Court had just held that Congress never gave the FDA authority to regulate tobacco, so Congress should amend the law to provide that authority.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce on April 6, 2000, and to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on April 17, 2000.

The sponsor gave introductory remarks on May 3, 2000, and those were the last entries in the bill's action history; no markup, vote, or further consideration ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
97 members cosponsored the bill: 69 Democrats, 27 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers are better off: with the bill dead and the Supreme Court's ruling standing, they faced no FDA regulation of their products or marketing, and tobacco growers kept their freedom from federal farm oversight. Had it become law, the public would have gained a regulator with power over how cigarettes are made and sold.

for.name: Rep. Greg Ganske
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 6, 2000, to write FDA authority over tobacco into law after the Supreme Court's ruling, and gave introductory remarks on May 3, 2000.

for.name: Rep. John Dingell
for.role: Original cosponsor, ranking Democrat on the Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor the day the bill was introduced.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Original cosponsor, senior Democrat on the Health and Environment Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee: after referral on April 6, 2000, no markup or hearing was scheduled and the bill died in subcommittee. He represented a Virginia tobacco district and chaired the committee through the 106th Congress.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Lorillard, and Brown & Williamson
against.what_they_did: Opposed FDA authority over tobacco, whose successful Supreme Court case the bill was written to overturn, and had long campaigned in Congress against FDA jurisdiction over their products.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: a Republican doctor led the bill and 27 of 222 House Republicans joined 69 of 205 House Democrats as cosponsors, though the committee chairman who never acted was also a Republican.

industries.note: The bill puts nicotine and tobacco products under FDA authority, restricts advertising and promotion, mandates stronger warnings, and bars 'reduced risk' claims the FDA has not verified. An unregulated market lets manufacturers market addictive products, including to young people, with no federal health regulator, which is exactly what the public loses in this outcome.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf and its producers from FDA authority and bars FDA staff from entering tobacco farms without written consent. The carve-out locks farm interests out of regulation even as manufacturers come under it, a concession designed to blunt farm-state opposition.
FDA sale-and-distribution restrictions would expressly cover tobacco advertising and promotion, shrinking a revenue stream built around selling a product that causes 400,000 deaths a year.
